acceptedAnswer.text: The final mile is the last leg of a freight journey: from the last facility — a port terminal, a warehouse, a regional hub — to the address where the item belongs. It is the only leg of the journey the recipient watches happen, and it is where a shipment that has traveled thousands of miles can still fail in the last fifty feet. In our operation the chain is unbroken: freight is unloaded on our own warehouse floor, counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, staged or deconsolidated, then delivered in by the same operation — no hand-off to an unknown last carrier.

Final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification. The published chain: freight is received and unloaded on our warehouse floor and counted as it crosses the dock; staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked, and reworked where needed; protected under the white-glove wrap standard; then delivered in on a planned route, set in its final position, its packaging removed as agreed, and its placement and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves.

Households and businesses needing final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification — retail and e-commerce operations whose big-and-bulky products cannot end at a curb, retailers whose customers expect the item in the room, manufacturers and importers landing freight through the Port of Virginia or Virginia Inland Port chain, designers, facility managers, and households receiving high-value, fragile or heavy items.

mainEntity.name: Will my delivery be left at the curb?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The published standard is the top of the delivery ladder: the item crosses the threshold, is set in its final position, its packaging is removed as agreed, and placement is verified with the recipient. Curbside and threshold-only tiers are not published as offers — the published standard starts inside the door.

Curbside (left at the curb or driveway); threshold (carried inside the first door, garage or lobby); room of choice (carried to the room the recipient picks, no unpacking); room of choice with packaging removal; and white glove (room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal). Some providers add assembly or installation at the top tier. The ladder is industry vocabulary — no regulator defines these names — which is why the confirmation list matters more than the label on the quote.

mainEntity.name: What should you confirm before you book?

acceptedAnswer.text: Confirm in writing, whichever level you are buying: the endpoint (curb, first door, or a named room — and whether stairs are included); unpacking; packaging removal and what it excludes; assembly and installation; the appointment, who must be present, and whether a signature is required; inspection at signing, with condition recorded before the paperwork is signed; and the failed-delivery answer — what happens, and who pays, if the item cannot be carried in.

mainEntity.name: Can a final-mile delivery be scheduled?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — appointment-based delivery is the norm for freight of any size, and our deliveries are arranged by appointment too. No fixed window length is published for this service — the appointment is set when the job is scoped and quoted.

mainEntity.name: Is final-mile delivery available for residences?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Our final-mile deliveries run to homes as well as to offices, industrial sites and retail spaces, dispatched from the Winchester and Martinsburg branches. A residence with stairs or a heavy piece is exactly the delivery to confirm in detail before the day.

mainEntity.name: Why does white-glove delivery cost more than curbside?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the service is different work, not a different label. The top tier carries two-person teams, the scheduling coordination of an appointment, the extra time to carry, place, unpack and inspect, and the liability management of handling heavy or high-value freight inside the building. A curbside price stops at the curb — and hands you the carry, the placement and the stair risk.

mainEntity.name: What should I check before I sign for a delivery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check the item in its final position before the paperwork is signed: finish, corners, doors and drawers, and whether it is complete. Note any damage on the delivery documents, not after the crew has gone. Our crews verify condition with you before they leave.

Sometimes in the industry — and only when it is agreed. Industry descriptions list assembly among the things white-glove service may include, and the scope depends on the carrier and the agreement, so it has to be confirmed before booking. On our side the answer is plain: assembly and installation are not part of our published final-mile scope. If a delivery turns on either, settle it with us when the job is scoped.

mainEntity.name: Is debris removal included with a delivery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Removing the delivered item's own packaging is one service; hauling away the old item it replaces is another, and the second is not implied by the first. Our published practice covers the delivered item's packaging — removed as agreed. Haul-away of old items is not published as part of our service.
